overview.title: How Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX relate, and the start of the TensorFlow introduction
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.section: 3.2 How these frameworks relate to each other
overview.main_topic: The split between low-level tensor frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX) and the high-level Keras API, Keras's need for a backend, and TensorFlow's release history
overview.central_idea: The four frameworks are not interchangeable. TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX provide low-level tensor manipulation (tensors and variables, tensor operations, backpropagation); Keras provides high-level concepts (layers combined into models, loss, optimizer, metrics, a training loop). Keras is not standalone: it needs a backend (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX, or NumPy for inference only). Section 3.3 then begins with TensorFlow, Google's framework released November 2015.
overview.importance: This two-level picture organizes the rest of chapter 3 and maps every piece of the chapter 2 from-scratch code onto the API layer it belongs to.
learning_objectives: Explain the difference between Keras (high level) and TensorFlow/PyTorch/JAX (low level) using the house-building analogy.
List the low-level concepts (tensors, variables, tensor operations, backpropagation) and the high-level ones (layers, model, loss, optimizer, metrics, training loop).
Explain why Keras needs a backend engine and why the NumPy backend cannot train.
State the order in which the chapter covers the frameworks and TensorFlow's main release dates.
prerequisites: Chapter 2's concepts: tensors, tensor operations, backpropagation, loss, optimizer, mini-batch SGD (pp.82-83)

paragraphs.excerpt: Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX don't all have the same feature set
paragraphs.what_it_says: The four frameworks are not interchangeable; they overlap but mostly serve different roles. The main divide is that Keras is high level and the others are low level. Keras is like a prefabricated building kit with a streamlined interface for setting up and training networks; TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are like raw construction materials.
paragraphs.what_it_means: You do not choose 'Keras or TensorFlow' as alternatives at the same level; you typically use Keras on top of one of the others. The low-level frameworks give you full control over every tensor operation; Keras packages common patterns (layers, training loops) so you rarely need that control.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This clears up a common confusion and frames the chapter: sections 3.3-3.5 teach the raw materials, section 3.6 the kit.

terminology.meaning: One that exposes abstractions like layers, models and training loops.
One that exposes tensors, tensor operations and gradient computation directly.

connections: p.86: Keras launched as a higher-level library on Theano

paragraphs.excerpt: First, low-level tensor manipulation—The infrastructure that underlies all modern machine learning.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduced by 'As you saw in the previous chapters, training a neural network revolves around the following concepts': first, low-level tensor manipulation, which translates to low-level APIs in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX: tensors (including variables that store the network's state), tensor operations such as addition, relu or matmul, and backpropagation, a way to compute gradients of mathematical expressions.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These are exactly the pieces of chapter 2: keras.Variable for W and b (p.77), ops.matmul, ops.relu and addition in NaiveDense, and tf.GradientTape for gradients (p.80). They are the materials every model is built from.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Each of sections 3.3-3.5 shows these three items (tensors/variables, operations, gradients) in one framework, so this list is the checklist for reading them.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Variables differ from ordinary tensors in being mutable state that persists across training steps and can be updated in place (w.assign on p.80).

terminology.meaning: A special tensor storing the network's state (its weights), updated in place during training.
A function on tensors such as addition, relu or matmul.
Here described as a way to compute the gradient of mathematical expressions.

connections: p.77: keras.Variable and ops.matmul in NaiveDense
p.83: backpropagation in the chapter 2 summary

paragraphs.excerpt: Second, high-level deep learning concepts—This translates to Keras APIs: – Layers, which
paragraphs.what_it_says: Second, high-level deep learning concepts, which translate to Keras APIs: layers combined into a model, a loss function defining the feedback signal, an optimizer determining how learning proceeds, metrics such as accuracy, and a training loop performing mini-batch stochastic gradient descent.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In chapter 2's from-scratch code these were NaiveDense (layer), NaiveSequential (model), sparse_categorical_crossentropy (loss), update_weights (optimizer), the argmax accuracy computation (metric) and fit() (training loop). Keras provides each of them ready-made.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It maps directly onto section 3.6 (layers, models, compile with loss/optimizer/metrics, fit) and onto the loss/optimizer pair stressed in the chapter 2 summary.

terminology.meaning: A quantity used to evaluate model performance (e.g. accuracy), not necessarily optimized directly.
The repeated cycle of batches and epochs performing mini-batch SGD.

connections: pp.78-82: the from-scratch equivalents of each concept

paragraphs.excerpt: Note that PyTorch is a bit of an intermediate case: while it
paragraphs.what_it_says: Footnote 2: PyTorch is an intermediate case; mainly lower level, it also includes its own layers and optimizers. But when you use PyTorch with Keras, you only interact with low-level PyTorch APIs such as tensor operations.
paragraphs.what_it_means: PyTorch has a high-level layer of its own (modules such as torch.nn.Linear and optimizers such as torch.optim.SGD), so it straddles the two categories. Under Keras, Keras supplies those high-level pieces and PyTorch is used only as the tensor engine.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It refines the clean two-level picture and anticipates section 3.4, where PyTorch's own layers and optimizers appear.

paragraphs.excerpt: Further, Keras is unique in that it isn't a fully standalone framework.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Keras is not fully standalone: it needs a backend engine, as a prefab kit must source materials. TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX can all be Keras backends. Keras can also run on NumPy, but because NumPy has no gradient API, Keras on NumPy can only make predictions; training is impossible.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The NumPy case shows precisely what Keras requires from a backend for training: automatic differentiation (feature 1 on p.85). Forward computation alone is enough for inference.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It makes the dependency concrete and explains why the backend choice matters, plus why Keras models can move between backends (p.86).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in Keras 3 the backend is chosen via the KERAS_BACKEND environment variable ("tensorflow", "jax", "torch" or "numpy") before importing keras.

terminology.meaning: The low-level framework that executes Keras's computations.
Using a model to make predictions, without training it.

connections: p.85: automatic differentiation as a key framework feature
p.86: existing Keras models can run on new frameworks via new backends

paragraphs.excerpt: Now that you have a clearer understanding of how all these frameworks came
paragraphs.what_it_says: Having seen how the frameworks arose and relate, the chapter turns to working with them, in chronological order: TensorFlow, then PyTorch, then JAX.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The order follows the history of p.86: TensorFlow late 2015, PyTorch about a year later, JAX a few years after that.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It tells you the structure of sections 3.3-3.5.

paragraphs.excerpt: TensorFlow is a Python-based open source machine learning framework developed primarily by
paragraphs.what_it_says: TensorFlow is a Python-based open source ML framework developed primarily by Google, released initially in November 2015, with v1 in February 2017 and v2 in October 2019; it is heavily used in production-grade ML across industry.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The dates match p.86's 'late 2015'. The emphasis on production use previews what section 3.3.3 will say is distinctive about TensorFlow.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It opens the first framework walk-through, which will show tensors, variables, operations and gradients in TensorFlow.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: TensorFlow 2 made eager execution the default (TensorFlow 1 required building a static graph and running it in a session).

terminology.meaning: Used in deployed, real-world systems rather than just research prototypes.

concepts.name: Keras backend
concepts.definition: The engine Keras needs to run: TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX (or NumPy for inference only).
concepts.intuition: The building materials a prefab kit is made from.
concepts.technical: Training requires a backend with a gradient API; NumPy lacks one, so Keras on NumPy can only predict.
concepts.significance: It makes Keras portable across frameworks.
concepts.example: Running the same Keras model with the JAX backend for training and the NumPy backend for predictions.
concepts.misconception: Keras is not a standalone framework.

concepts.name: Low-level tensor manipulation
concepts.definition: The infrastructure layer of tensors (including variables), tensor operations and backpropagation, provided by TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.
concepts.technical: Corresponds to keras.Variable, ops.matmul / ops.relu and tf.GradientTape in the chapter 2 code.
concepts.significance: Everything high-level is built from it.
concepts.misconception: Low level does not mean slow or obsolete; it means more explicit control.

concepts.name: High-level deep learning concepts (Keras APIs)
concepts.definition: Layers combined into a model, a loss function, an optimizer, metrics and a training loop performing mini-batch SGD.
concepts.technical: Covered in section 3.6: layers, models, compile, loss choice, fit, validation, inference.
concepts.significance: This is the level at which most of the book's code is written.
concepts.example: From scratch: NaiveDense, NaiveSequential, crossentropy, update_weights, accuracy, fit() (pp.77-82).
concepts.misconception: A metric is not the same as the loss; accuracy evaluates, the loss trains.

concepts.name: Variable
concepts.definition: A special tensor that stores a network's state (its weights) and can be modified in place.
concepts.intuition: A labelled container whose contents the optimizer keeps rewriting.
concepts.technical: keras.Variable in NaiveDense (p.77), updated with w.assign (p.80).
concepts.significance: Distinguishes learnable state from transient computation results.
concepts.misconception: Ordinary tensors produced by operations are not variables and are not updated by the optimizer.

deeper.title: Mapping chapter 2's from-scratch code onto the two levels
deeper.body:
| Concept on this page | Level | From-scratch code (pp.77-82) |
|---|---|---|
| Tensors / variables | low | `keras.Variable` for `W`, `b` |
| Tensor operations | low | `ops.matmul`, `+ self.b`, `ops.relu`, `ops.softmax` |
| Backpropagation | low | `tf.GradientTape`, `tape.gradient` |
| Layers, model | high | `NaiveDense`, `NaiveSequential` |
| Loss function | high | `ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy` |
| Optimizer | high | `update_weights` / `optimizers.SGD` |
| Metrics | high | `argmax` + `==` + `mean` accuracy |
| Training loop | high | `fit()` with `BatchGenerator` |

The table is our own arrangement of the page's lists.

deeper.title: Why NumPy can run Keras but not train it
deeper.body:
1. Prediction needs only the forward pass: matmuls, additions and activations, which NumPy provides.
2. Training needs gradients of the loss with respect to every variable.
3. NumPy has no API to compute gradients automatically (p.87), so step 2 is impossible.
4. Hence Keras on NumPy is restricted to inference. This mirrors p.85: autodiff is the first of the three features a framework must provide.

misconceptions.claim: Keras and TensorFlow are competing alternatives at the same level.
misconceptions.correction: Keras is high level and runs on a low-level backend such as TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX.

misconceptions.claim: Keras can train models on any backend, including NumPy.
misconceptions.correction: NumPy has no gradient API, so Keras on NumPy can only make predictions.

misconceptions.claim: PyTorch is purely a low-level framework.
misconceptions.correction: Footnote 2: it also has its own layers and optimizers, though with Keras you only use its low-level APIs.
Its initial release was November 2015; v1 came in February 2017 and v2 in October 2019.

takeaways: Keras is high level (a prefab kit); TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are low level (raw materials).
Low level: tensors and variables, tensor operations, backpropagation. High level: layers and models, loss, optimizer, metrics, training loop.
Keras needs a backend: TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX; NumPy works for predictions only, because it cannot compute gradients.
PyTorch is an intermediate case with its own layers and optimizers.
The chapter covers TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX in chronological order; TensorFlow was released November 2015 (v1 Feb 2017, v2 Oct 2019).

questions.question: In the book's house-building analogy, what does Keras correspond to?
options: The land the house is built on
questions.explanation: Keras provides a streamlined interface for setting up and training networks, like a prefab kit. TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are the raw materials. The other two options are not in the analogy.

questions.question: Which of these belongs to the low-level tensor manipulation layer rather than to the high-level Keras concepts?
questions.explanation: The page lists tensors/variables, tensor operations and backpropagation as low-level; optimizer, metrics and training loop are high-level Keras concepts.

questions.question: Why can Keras running on the NumPy backend make predictions but not train a model?
questions.answer: NumPy provides no API for gradients, and training requires computing gradients of the loss with respect to the weights.
questions.explanation: Prediction needs only the forward computation; training needs automatic differentiation, which NumPy lacks.

questions.question: Map each piece of the chapter 2 from-scratch code to the page's concept lists: keras.Variable, ops.matmul, tf.GradientTape, NaiveSequential, update_weights, fit().
questions.answer: keras.Variable: tensors/variables (low). ops.matmul: tensor operations (low). tf.GradientTape: backpropagation (low). NaiveSequential: layers combined into a model (high). update_weights: optimizer (high). fit(): training loop (high).
questions.explanation: The page says training revolves around these concepts 'as you saw in the previous chapters'; the from-scratch code implemented each one explicitly.

questions.question: Why does footnote 2 call PyTorch an intermediate case?
questions.answer: Because, although mainly low level, it includes its own layers and optimizers; with Keras, though, you only use its low-level APIs.

questions.question: Give TensorFlow's initial, v1 and v2 release dates.
questions.answer: Initial release November 2015; v1 February 2017; v2 October 2019.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of section 3.3.

questions.question: Can you explain to someone why 'Should I learn Keras or TensorFlow?' is a slightly malformed question?
questions.answer: They are at different levels: Keras is a high-level API that runs on top of a low-level backend like TensorFlow (or PyTorch or JAX), so you typically use both together.
questions.explanation: This is the central point of section 3.2.
